title: MASC-ED: Masculinity and diversity in eating disorders – a pilot study
summary: There is currently only limited scientific knowledge about eating disorders in men and in people from sexual and gender minority groups (LGBTQIA+). In particular, there is a lack of research on how eating disorders develop, how they present, and how they are maintained in these groups. As an increasing number of men are affected by eating disorders and this can be associated with stigmatization, the MASC-ED study examines the role of biological sex, gender, and sexual orientation in eating disorders. This study includes a quantitative and a qualitative part. In the quantitative part, cisgender men and cisgender women with an eating disorder are compared. Using standardized questionnaires, diagnostic interviews, and computer-based neuropsychological tasks, the study examines whether these groups differ with regard to the development, symptoms, and maintenance of eating disorders. In addition, differences depending on the type of eating disorder are examined, particularly between predominantly restrictive eating behavior and eating disorders with regular binge eating. The qualitative part of the current study is aimed at people with diverse gender identities and sexual orientations. In semi-structured interviews, experiences with eating disorders are explored, including symptoms, course of illness, body image, and experiences of stigmatization. MASC-ED thereby aims to improve understanding of differences in eating disorders related to sex, gender, and sexual and gender identity. The findings are intended to contribute to a fairer and more inclusive understanding of eating disorders, help reduce stigma, and, in the long term, support the development of individually tailored treatment approaches.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Diagnosis of an eating disorder 
- Minimum age 18 years
- Written informed consent
- Sufficient German or English language proficiency (at least B2 level)
Exclusion criteria:
- Acute suicidality
- Suspicion of a psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, severe substance use disorder, or other  severe mental disorders according to the DSM-5 (SCID-5-CV; Beesdo-Baum et al., 2019)
- Neurological illnesses or medications that affect information processing in the brain
- Pregnancy or breastfeeding
- Insufficient German or English language skills (participants must be able to communicate spontaneously and fluently enough to hold an everyday conversation with native speakers without significant effort on either side, i.e., at B2 level)
